extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for examining claim limitations that invoke 35 U.S.C. 112(f) (or pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, sixth paragraph), including when to reject under 35 U.S.C. 112(b)/pre‑AIA second paragraph and how to assess specification support (structure, algorithm, drawings, incorporation by reference, linkage to function, written description/enablement).

rubrics_metrics.name: Invocation of 35 U.S.C. 112(f) (means/step‑plus‑function)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether a claim limitation is a means‑ (or step‑) plus‑function limitation invoking 35 U.S.C. 112(f) (or pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, sixth paragraph). If it is unclear whether the limitation falls within the scope of 112(f), a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (or pre‑AIA second paragraph) may be appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If ambiguous whether the claim language invokes 112(f), treat ambiguity as a potential basis for indefiniteness rejection under 112(b). Example: claims using 'means' or 'step' typically invoke 112(f) but context can negate invocation; examiner should make a determination and, if unclear, consider 112(b) rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification must disclose corresponding structure/material/acts
rubrics_metrics.description: A means‑plus‑function limitation must have its corresponding structure (or material or acts) disclosed in the specification itself in a way that one skilled in the art will understand what structure will perform the recited function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclosure can be explicit in text or in drawings/figures. The test is whether one of ordinary skill would understand the specification itself to disclose the structure that performs the recited function (Atmel; Dossel). If no such disclosure exists, the claim fails 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (pre‑AIA second paragraph).

rubrics_metrics.name: Implicit/inherent disclosure allowed but bare 'known techniques' language is insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: The corresponding structure may be implicit or inherent in the specification if it would have been clear to those skilled in the art, but a bare statement that known techniques or methods can be used does not disclose structure for means‑plus‑function limitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti‑pattern: phrasing like 'may be controlled by known differential pressure, valving and control equipment' is insufficient (Biomedino). If the disclosure only states that known techniques may be used, treat as no corresponding structure disclosed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Means‑plus‑function invocation does not excuse compliance with 112(a) or 112(b)
rubrics_metrics.description: Invoking 35 U.S.C. 112(f) (or pre‑AIA sixth paragraph) does not exempt an applicant from the written description (112(a)/pre‑AIA first paragraph) or definiteness (112(b)/pre‑AIA second paragraph) requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even with means‑plus‑function language, the specification must adequately describe and particularly point out the invention; courts have rejected any reading that creates an exception to written description or definiteness (Donaldson; Knowlton).

rubrics_metrics.name: Drawings can provide written description of corresponding structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Drawings, figures, tables or sequence listings in the original disclosure may provide the written description sufficient to identify corresponding structure for a means‑plus‑function limitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Vas‑Cath recognized drawings can satisfy written description. Examiner should consider drawings as part of the disclosure when determining if corresponding structure is present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computer‑implemented means‑plus‑function requires disclosure of an algorithm
rubrics_metrics.description: When the disclosed structure is a computer programmed to carry out an algorithm, the corresponding structure is the special purpose computer as programmed to perform the disclosed algorithm; the specification must disclose the algorithm for performing the claimed function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A general purpose computer alone is not sufficient for a specific computer‑implemented function; the specification must disclose an algorithm (e.g., prose, math formula, flowchart, source code or other adequate description) that transforms a general purpose processor into the special purpose computer (Aoyama; WMS; Aristocrat; Noah).

rubrics_metrics.name: General purpose computer is sufficient only for general computing functions
rubrics_metrics.description: A general purpose computer may be adequate corresponding structure when the recited function is a general computing function (e.g., 'means for storing data'), but for claiming a specific function a general purpose computer without an algorithm is insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claimed functions (e.g., 'processing,' 'receiving,' 'storing') are truly coextensive with a general purpose processor's structure, additional algorithm disclosure may not be required (Katz example). Otherwise, require algorithm disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algorithm disclosure must be sufficient to perform the entire claimed function
rubrics_metrics.description: If an algorithm is disclosed, its sufficiency is judged by whether one of ordinary skill in the art would understand it to define the structure and enable performance of the entire claimed function; an algorithm that supports only part of the function is inadequate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the algorithm covers some but not all functional components, treat the specification as if no algorithm were disclosed and consider a 112(b) rejection. Importing off‑the‑shelf software or asserting that skilled artisans could fill gaps does not cure an inadequate algorithm (Noah; Finisar).

rubrics_metrics.name: One skilled in the art's knowledge does not replace required disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Argument that a person of ordinary skill could write the software or otherwise implement the function does not relieve the patentee/applicant of the duty to disclose sufficient structure (algorithm) in the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases (Blackboard; Biomedino; Atmel) emphasize that relying on the skill of artisans is not a substitute for disclosing specific structure or algorithm. Examiner should not accept mere assertions that skilled artisans could implement the invention without sufficient specification detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mode of implementation limits claim scope (hardware vs software)
rubrics_metrics.description: By using means‑plus‑function language an applicant limits the claim to the disclosed structure/implementation (e.g., hardware or hardware+software) and equivalents; the examiner should not construe the limitation to cover pure software implementation if the spec discloses hardware or hardware+software structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If no corresponding structure is disclosed (only software per se without algorithm), the limitation should be deemed indefinite and rejected under 112(b). Claims must be read as a whole: a claim with a means limitation lacking structural support is not necessarily directed to software per se unless other claim limitations also point that way.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supporting disclosure must clearly link/associate structure to claimed function
rubrics_metrics.description: The written description or prosecution history must clearly link or associate the disclosed structure, material, or acts to the function recited in the means‑ (or step‑) plus‑function limitation for that disclosure to qualify as the corresponding structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This 'clear link' requirement is the quid pro quo for using means‑plus‑function claiming. If one of ordinary skill cannot identify what in the specification performs the claimed function, a 112(b) rejection is appropriate (B. Braun; Medical Instrumentation & Diagnostics).

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner procedure: determine function and then identify corresponding structure in spec
rubrics_metrics.description: Once a limitation is determined to be means‑plus‑function invoking 112(f), the examiner must determine the claimed function and review the written description (including drawings, figures, tables, sequence listings) to identify corresponding structure, material, or acts disclosed in the original specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The corresponding structure must be disclosed in the application itself; structures present only in incorporated‑by‑reference material or prior art are not valid corresponding structures (Pressure Prods.; Atmel). Review disclosure from the viewpoint of a person skilled in the art (Tech. Licensing; Med. Instrumentation).

rubrics_metrics.name: When rejection under 112(b) is appropriate (enumerated situations)
rubrics_metrics.description: A rejection under 112(b) (pre‑AIA second paragraph) may be appropriate: (1) when it is unclear whether a claim limitation invokes 112(f); (2) when 112(f) is invoked and there is no disclosure or insufficient disclosure of corresponding structure/material/acts; and/or (3) when 112(f) is invoked and the supporting disclosure fails to clearly link/associate the disclosed structure/material/acts to the claimed function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the examiner cannot identify corresponding structure/material/acts, make a 112(b) rejection. The MPEP lists these three distinct circumstances as triggers for a 112(b) rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedure when spec relies on incorporated‑by‑reference material
rubrics_metrics.description: If corresponding structure is described in broad generic terms and specific details are incorporated by reference, Office personnel must review the specification itself (without relying on the incorporated document) and apply the 'one skilled in the art' analysis to determine whether the specification identifies the corresponding structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If one skilled in the art could identify the structure from the specification alone, 112(b) is satisfied (Dossel example). If not, the applicant should be required to amend the specification to include the relevant portions of the referenced document (37 CFR 1.57(c)(3)); applicant need only insert the portions relevant to the means‑plus‑function limitation (Atmel).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of 37 CFR 1.105 / requirement for information when corresponding structure unknown
rubrics_metrics.description: If the examiner cannot identify the corresponding structure/material/acts, a requirement for information under 37 CFR 1.105 may be made to require the identification; if the applicant states lack of such information or fails to identify the corresponding structure, a 112(b) rejection should be made and failure to reply may result in abandonment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP § 704.11(a) Example R and MPEP § 704.12 for guidance on replies to requirements for information and consequences of failure to reply within time period (including extensions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific disclosure in specific terms satisfies 112(b) and 112(f)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the corresponding structure/material/acts are described in the specification in specific terms (e.g., an emitter‑coupled voltage comparator), are linked to the claimed function and one skilled in the art could identify them as adequate to perform the recited function, then 112(b) and 112(f) requirements are satisfied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete, specific structural descriptions linked to the function (Atmel example) satisfy definiteness — no need to import additional material.

rubrics_metrics.name: If one skilled in the art cannot identify structure, applicant must amend specification (limited insertion)
rubrics_metrics.description: If one skilled in the art would not be able to identify the corresponding structure/material/acts from the specification, the applicant should be required to amend the specification to include the relevant portions of any referenced document so that the structure and its link to the function are present.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicant should not be required to insert the entirety of the referenced document; only include relevant portions corresponding to the means‑plus‑function limitation (Atmel; 37 CFR 1.57(c)(3)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Means‑plus‑function claims must also meet 112(a) (written description/enablement)
rubrics_metrics.description: A means‑plus‑function limitation found indefinite for lacking corresponding structure may also lack adequate written description and/or enablement under 112(a); the specification must demonstrate possession of the claimed invention, especially for genus/functionally defined claims which must be supported by species sufficient to justify the genus (Ariad).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing 112(a) support consider original disclosure in summary, detailed description, original claims, abstract, and drawings. Genus claims defined by function require evidence of species to support the breadth claimed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not import unrecited functional or unnecessary structural limitations from the specification into claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Functional limitations not recited in the claim, or structural limitations from the written description that are unnecessary to perform the claimed function, cannot be imported into the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims must be construed to cover the disclosed corresponding structure and its equivalents, but examiners/applicants should not read extra functional or structural limitations from the spec into the claim (Welker Bearing; Wenger).
